note_tweet.text:
Was blown away by this Gond Art-inspired, absolutely magnificent masterpiece from Salt Lake FD Block . This Pandal is a brilliant exercise in the tribal art of the Gond community of Chhattisgarh. 

Prasanta Pal has created magic with the dots and dashes that adorn their mudhouse walls and floors. He has also used fish scales and other signature patterns to fill animal and plant shapes as well as sacred trees like the Tree of Life, with herbivores at the base of the food chain and omnivores towards the top.  

Natural elements like charcoal (black), leaves (green) and different types of soil have been used. Organic items from nature like sal leaves, hogla leaves, donga, coir, hanging roots of trees, the main axis of coconut clusters, bamboo slices and more have been collected from villages over months for use here. 

It is a treat to study each section.  If there are dots and dashes on sal leaves at the entrance, there are birds and flowers using small wicker baskets overhead and elephants made of bark of date palm trees, cane and bamboo slices on the walls. Leaves of ashwattha trees have been used to create a cluster of peacock feathers. The idol of Maa is also crafted using the same art form.  

The sheer vision and scale here is simply put – dazzling. To even imagine and put it together – how much time and effort it must have taken!  But when it comes to celebrating Maa – anything is possible I guess.

#DurgaPuja2026 #DurgaPujaFestival2026 #MaaDurga #JaiMaaDurga #Navami

note_tweet.text:
In the 1890s, a Dalit man in a village in Chhattisgarh was stopped at a temple door. So he tattooed the name of Ram on his forehead.

His name was Parasuram. He was from Charpora village.

They could stop him from entering the temple. They could not stop the name of Ram from being on his body.

Others from his community did the same. They became known as the Ramnami Samaj. Some tattooed Ram on their forehead. Some covered their entire body, even their eyelids, with the name of Ram. They are called purnanakshik.

Upper caste Hindus went to court to stop them from using Ram's name. In 1910, the Ramnamis won.

Even in the 1980s, tattooed Ramnamis were still being turned away from temples.

Today most of the full body tattooed Ramnamis are in their seventies. Many young Ramnamis don't get tattooed anymore. They fear they will be discriminated against and won't get work.

This Durga Puja, the Chaltabagan pandal in Kolkata made them its theme. They called it Nishan, The Mark. Ramnami members were invited to unveil it.

One of them, Seth Bai, said, "All communities should co-exist in peace and brotherhood."
